Infectious Disorders of the CNSDisease Index — Neurology

🧠

How Infection Reaches & Damages the CNS

Orienting framework for every disease in this section — not itself a graded LO, so no vignette or quiz here. Refer back to this whenever a workup or pathophysiology question turns on how an organism got in or why it's causing damage.

Four Routes of Entry into the CNS

1Hematogenous

Most common route — typically arterial ("embolic") seeding. Infection entering the venous system (e.g. of the face or sinuses) can also flow retrograde via anastomoses with the cerebral venous circulation into the CNS.

2Direct Implantation

Via trauma or iatrogenic introduction — classically, lumbar puncture.

3Contiguous Spread

Direct extension from an infected site nearby — commonly the mastoid or frontal sinuses, an infected tooth, or an infected cranial/spinal surgical site.

4Neural Transport

Viral infection of the peripheral nervous system (e.g. Herpes virus, rabies) travels with extension from the dorsal root ganglion into the spinal cord.

Mechanisms of Infectious CNS Damage
Pathophysiology
  • Direct infection and injury of neurons, glia, or endothelial cells by the organism itself
  • Microbial toxins and the downstream effects of the host's own inflammatory response
  • Post-infectious immune-related injury — damage driven by the immune system after the acute infection, rather than the organism directly
Why This Matters Going Forward

Every disease in this section fits one or more of these four entry routes and three injury mechanisms — e.g. bacterial meningitis is classically hematogenous with direct pyogenic/inflammatory injury, while herpes encephalitis is a neural-transport infection with direct neuronal injury. Keep this framework in mind as a differentiating lens between conditions.

🧫

Acute Bacterial Meningitis

LO 1–6 Medical Emergency CSF: ↓Glucose ↑Protein ↑PMNs Empiric Abx First
How boards would word it

"A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of high fever, severe headache, and confusion. His wife reports he has vomited twice and cannot tolerate light. Temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F), he is lethargic but arousable, and passive neck flexion produces involuntary knee flexion (Kernig's sign). A petechial rash is noted on his lower extremities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"

Answer: Draw blood cultures and start empiric IV antibiotics (± dexamethasone) immediately — do not delay treatment for imaging or LP
What to look for: acute fever + headache + photophobia + meningismus (Kernig's sign) is the core triad-plus for bacterial meningitis, and the petechial rash points toward N. meningitidis. This combination makes it a medical emergency — antibiotics must never be delayed while waiting on confirmatory LP or imaging.
▶
▶ Meningitis - causes, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, pathology
Video — "Meningitis - causes, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, pathology" (YouTube)
LO1 — Natural History
Epidemiology & Etiology

Low incidence (~0.025/1,000) but a medical emergency whenever it occurs. Entry into undisturbed cerebral structures is via hematogenous spread or extension from cranial structures (ears, eyes, paranasal sinuses); iatrogenic/traumatic entry occurs when tissue is directly disturbed. Predisposing conditions: mastoiditis, otitis, sinusitis.

By Age / Risk Group

  • Neonates: Group B Streptococcus, E. coli
  • Adults overall: S. pneumoniae (50%), N. meningitidis (25%), Group B strep (15%)
  • Children/young adults <20: N. meningitidis (60%)
  • Elderly / immunocompromised: Listeria monocytogenes (<10% of adult cases overall, but disproportionately here)
  • H. influenzae — far less common since routine vaccination
  • Nosocomial infections: Staphylococcus and gram-negative bacteria account for ~40%

Spread Once Inside

Infection can extend down the Virchow-Robin spaces — thin extensions of the subarachnoid space surrounding penetrating vessels — though these do not carry infection far into the parenchyma.

LO2 — Clinical Presentation

Adults

  • Acute-to-subacute onset
  • Classic triad: fever, headache, nuchal rigidity
  • Meningeal irritation signs: Kernig's, Brudzinski's
  • Raised ICP, nausea/vomiting, photophobia, convulsions, disordered consciousness

Infants & Newborns

  • Fever, irritability, drowsiness, vomiting
  • Convulsions
  • Bulging fontanel
  • Lethargic or "floppy" baby
Red Flag

Classic meningismus can be subtle or absent in infants and the elderly — a bulging fontanel or unexplained lethargy in an infant, or altered mentation alone in an elderly patient, should trigger the same urgency as the adult triad.

LO3 — Diagnostic Workup
CSF ParameterNormalBacterialViral (aseptic)
AppearanceClearCloudy / purulentClear or slightly turbid
Opening pressure5–20 cmH₂OElevatedNormal to mildly elevated
WBC count0–5/mm³Markedly elevated (up to ~90,000/mm³), neutrophil-predominant10–1,000/mm³, lymphocyte-predominant
Protein15–45 mg/dLMarkedly elevatedMildly-to-moderately elevated
Glucose50–80 mg/dL (CSF:serum >0.6)Markedly decreasedNormal
Gram stain / cultureNegativeOften positive for organismNegative
Pearl

A decreased CSF glucose is extremely suspicious for bacterial meningitis — this is the single most useful CSF value for distinguishing it from viral causes.

Additional workup: blood cultures (drawn before antibiotics, though antibiotics should never be delayed for LP/imaging), CBC, chest film, CT (bone window) or MRI with gadolinium for suspected cerebral complications.

LO4 — Treatment
Approach

Medical emergency. First priority is hemodynamic support and treatment of septic shock if present. Empiric IV antibiotics are started immediately — begun while awaiting culture/LP results, never delayed for imaging. Steroids (dexamethasone) should be given before or at the same time as the first antibiotic dose, not after.

Empiric Antibiotics by Age/Risk Group

  • Neonates: ampicillin + cefotaxime (or gentamicin) — covers GBS, E. coli, Listeria
  • 1 month–adult: ceftriaxone (Rocephin) + vancomycin
  • Add ampicillin for age >50 or immunocompromised, to cover Listeria

Adjuncts

  • Dexamethasone: reduces mortality/complications, especially pneumococcal meningitis in adults — timing relative to antibiotics is critical (de Gans & van de Beek, NEJM 2002)
  • Acyclovir is added empirically if HSV encephalitis cannot be excluded
LO5 — Monitoring & Complications
Follow-Up & Long-Term Sequelae

Audiology testing before discharge (hearing loss is common), repeat neuroimaging if not improving clinically (evaluate for abscess, hydrocephalus, subdural effusion), and structured neurologic follow-up.

  • Decreased intellect, memory impairment
  • Seizures
  • Hearing loss, dizziness, gait imbalance
  • Hydrocephalus (non-obstructive/communicating, from healing-stage fibrosis)
  • Chronic adhesive arachnoiditis, chronic meningomyelitis
  • Stroke (from venous thrombosis or obliterative endarteritis of inflamed vessels)
LO6 — Prevention & Health Promotion
Vaccination & Prophylaxis
  • Vaccines: Hib (routine childhood), pneumococcal conjugate/polysaccharide (at-risk and elderly), meningococcal ACWY (routine adolescent) and MenB (at-risk/outbreak settings, college students)
  • Maternal GBS screening with intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent neonatal disease
  • Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts of confirmed meningococcal or Hib cases — rifampin, ceftriaxone, or ciprofloxacin for meningococcal contacts; rifampin for Hib contacts (esp. unvaccinated young children in the household)
Pearl

Before antibiotics, this disease was often fatal. Steroids and antibiotics are now given together (or steroids first) — reversing that order loses much of the mortality benefit of dexamethasone.

Acute Viral Meningitis

LO 1–6 Usually Enteroviral CSF: Lymphocytic, Normal Glucose Self-Limited
How boards would word it

"A 22-year-old college student presents in August with 2 days of fever, headache, and photophobia. She denies confusion, focal weakness, or seizures. Neurologic exam is normal except for nuchal rigidity. Lumbar puncture reveals WBC 180/mm³ with 90% lymphocytes, protein 65 mg/dL, and glucose 58 mg/dL (serum glucose 95 mg/dL). Gram stain shows no organisms. Which of the following is the most likely etiology?"

Answer: Enterovirus
What to look for: summer seasonality plus lymphocyte-predominant pleocytosis with a preserved CSF:serum glucose ratio (~0.6) and a negative Gram stain points away from bacterial and toward viral (aseptic) meningitis — enteroviruses are by far the most common cause. The explicit absence of seizures/focal deficits argues against encephalitis.
▶
▶ Acute Viral Meningitis | Clinical Manifestations and Etiology
Video — "Acute Viral Meningitis | Clinical Manifestations and Etiology" (YouTube)
LO1 — Natural History
Epidemiology & Etiology

Marked seasonal variation — incidence up to 0.01/1,000 in summer/early fall (true incidence is likely underestimated since many mild cases go unreported). Enteroviruses cause 75–90% of cases overall, and ~80% of cases where an agent is actually identified (an agent is identified in only 60–90% of cases). Other causes: arbovirus, HSV-2, VZV, EBV, HIV, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus.

Pathogenesis — viral entry, primary infection, viremia, and secondary CNS invasion via BBB permeability + immune cell activation
Inhalation (mumps, EV-D68) or oral-fecal route (enterovirus)
→
Primary infection (respiratory / GI tract)
→
Viremia
→
Secondary infection (lymphoid tissue, choroid plexus, peripheral sensory neurons)
→
CNS entry (↑BBB permeability, interleukin/immune cell activation)
Pathology

Few, if any, cytological changes are seen in the nervous tissue itself. Inflammation is largely confined to the meninges, with a lymphocytic pleocytosis — this is the key pathologic distinction from the pyogenic destruction seen in bacterial meningitis.

Specific Viral Etiologies

Arboviral Encephalitis

RNA viruses transmitted by mosquito (occasionally tick) vectors, causing epidemic outbreaks; they do not form inclusions in infected cells. Examples: Eastern & Western equine encephalitis, St. Louis, Venezuelan, California types.

Herpes Simplex Virus

HSV-1: acute encephalitis in children/young adults (and AIDS patients); enters axonal terminals of the trigeminal nerve at an oral lesion, travels retrograde to the trigeminal ganglion where it can stay latent for years. Necrotizing, often hemorrhagic involvement of the medial temporal lobes/base of brain; perivascular lymphocytic cuffs and Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusions. HSV-2: usually a diffuse viral meningitis rather than encephalitis; neonates infected via vaginal delivery can develop severe acute encephalitis.

Varicella-Zoster Virus

Primary infection ("chickenpox") is typically benign in children. Virus remains latent for years in dorsal root ganglia, reactivating along a dermatome as "shingles." CNS involvement is rare — cerebral/meningeal granulomatous arteritis, or in immunosuppressed patients, severe multifocal necrotizing encephalitis with visible inclusions.

HIV-1

Up to 60% of AIDS patients develop neurologic dysfunction; ~90% show neuropathologic changes at autopsy. HIV meningitis can occur 1–2 weeks after seroconversion (~10% of patients) as a mild lymphocytic meningitis. HIV-1 encephalitis ("AIDS-related dementia"/cognitive-motor complex) presents insidiously with apathy, mental slowness, memory loss, ataxia, incontinence, seizures; imaging shows cortical atrophy and ventriculomegaly; pathology shows microglial nodules, neuronophagia, and multinucleated giant cells. Vacuolar myelopathy (~30% of AIDS spinal cords) resembles subacute combined degeneration. Cranial/peripheral neuropathies and myopathies (including AZT-associated) also occur. Congenital pediatric AIDS can cause microcephaly, mental retardation, and basal ganglia/white matter calcification.

LO2 — Clinical Presentation
Presentation
  • Fever
  • Headache
  • Signs of meningeal irritation
Red Flag

Seizures or focal neurologic deficits suggest encephalitis rather than isolated meningitis — this should broaden the workup (consider HSV specifically) and change management.

LO3 — Diagnostic Workup
CSF ParameterNormalViral (aseptic)Bacterial
Cell count0–5/mm³↑ Lymphocyte-predominantMarkedly ↑, neutrophil-predominant
Protein15–45 mg/dLModerately elevatedMarkedly elevated
Glucose50–80 mg/dLNormalMarkedly decreased
Gram stain / cultureNegativeNegativeOften positive

Differentiating from bacterial meningitis is the critical first step. Additional workup: PCR (increasingly the standard for enteroviral/HSV detection), serologic studies when appropriate, CBC with differential.

LO4 — Treatment
Approach

Primarily symptomatic/supportive — analgesics/antipyretics, hydration, antiemetics as needed. If HSV meningoencephalitis cannot be excluded on clinical grounds, IV acyclovir is started empirically while awaiting confirmatory testing, given how treatable — and how dangerous if missed — HSV encephalitis is.

LO5 — Monitoring & Complications
Prognosis & Sequelae

Prognosis is generally excellent. Rare persistent complications: headaches, mild mental impairment, imbalance, asthenia. Outcome in pediatric cases (<1 year) is less optimistic, with a higher risk of:

  • Intellectual impairment
  • Hearing loss
  • Learning disabilities
LO6 — Prevention & Health Promotion
Risk Reduction
  • Hand hygiene / enteric precautions to limit fecal-oral enterovirus transmission
  • Mosquito/tick vector control and avoidance for arboviral causes
  • Varicella and shingles vaccination to reduce primary VZV infection and reactivation risk
  • Antiretroviral therapy to prevent HIV-associated CNS disease
  • Safer sexual practices and suppressive antiviral therapy to reduce HSV-2 transmission

Poliomyelitis

LO 1–6 Anterior Horn / LMN Fecal-Oral Spread Vaccine-Preventable
How boards would word it

"A 6-year-old unvaccinated boy who recently returned from Pakistan presents with 3 days of fever and sore throat that resolved on its own. Five days later, he develops fever, severe leg pain, and progressive asymmetric weakness of the left leg, and is now unable to bear weight. Examination shows decreased deep tendon reflexes, hypotonia, and preserved sensation in the affected limb. Which of the following findings would most support the diagnosis?"

Answer: CSF pleocytosis with elevated protein and normal glucose
What to look for: a biphasic illness — mild GI/flu-like prodrome, a symptom-free interval, then asymmetric flaccid paralysis with preserved sensation — in an unvaccinated child from an endemic country is classic for poliomyelitis. Preserved sensation and asymmetry are the key distractor-busters against Guillain-Barré syndrome, which is typically symmetric and does not produce significant CSF pleocytosis (albuminocytologic dissociation instead).
▶
▶ Poliomyelitis (Poliovirus)
Video — "Poliomyelitis (Poliovirus)" (YouTube)
LO1 — Natural History
Epidemiology
  • Poliovirus is an RNA virus in the Picornaviridae family, genus Enterovirus — humans are the only known reservoir
  • Highly contagious; spread almost exclusively by the fecal-oral route (droplet spread is rare); incubation 7–14 days
  • Vaccination has reduced transmission by >99%; remains endemic only in Afghanistan and Pakistan
  • Vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 (VDPV2): live OPV replicates in a recently vaccinated person → reverts to neurovirulence → can cause paralytic disease in unvaccinated or immunocompromised close contacts
  • Risk factors: travel to/residence in endemic regions, laboratory work with poliovirus specimens, caring for likely-infected individuals (healthcare workers, refugee camp workers), being underimmunized/immunosuppressed, close contact with recent OPV recipients (e.g. international adoptees)
Pathogenesis
Oral ingestion
→
Binds CD155 on epithelial cells/neurons
→
Replication in pharyngeal/GI mucosa
→
Lymphatic spread → viremia
→
CNS invasion (~1% of cases)
→
Destruction of anterior horn α-motor neurons
Spinal cord cross-section — poliomyelitis/SMA selectively destroys the anterior (ventral) horn, sparing the lateral corticospinal tracts; ALS additionally involves the lateral columns (mixed UMN + LMN disease)
Pathology

Necrotic loss of α-motor neurons in the ventral horn of the spinal cord, with attack by microglia and lymphocytes causing neuronophagia, motor neuron loss, and gliosis. A mixed acute-and-chronic meningitis and myelitis of the spinal cord and brainstem (rarely the brain) may accompany this; viral spread to the dorsal root ganglia/dorsal horn has been reported but is less typical.

Lower vs. Upper Motor Neuron Disease
Lower Motor Neuron (e.g. Polio, ALS)Upper Motor Neuron (e.g. Stroke, MS)
Weakness patternIndividual muscles affectedMuscle groups affected
AtrophyPronounced ("wasting")Slight, disuse-related
ToneFlaccid / hypotonicSpastic
ReflexesDiminished/absent DTRsHyperactive DTRs
FasciculationsPresentAbsent
LO2 — Clinical Presentation
Overall Case Breakdown

>72% of infections are asymptomatic; <24% cause clinical (mostly flu-like) illness; <1% of infected individuals develop paralysis.

Abortive Poliomyelitis

Nonspecific gastroenteritis, fever, nausea, sore throat, myalgia, headache for 1–3 days. Complete recovery without complications, or transitions to CNS involvement.

Nonparalytic (Meningitic)

Begins after a symptom-free interval following the abortive phase: fever, neck stiffness, headache, vomiting, muscle pain. Head drop sign (neck muscle weakness) — but no paresis.

Paralytic Poliomyelitis

2–3 days after the meningitic form: fever, malaise, severe back/neck/muscle pain, then asymmetric acute flaccid paralysis worsening over hours-to-days — legs most common, proximal > distal. Diminished DTRs, atrophy, hypotonia, fasciculations. Muscle weakness typically begins 2–5 days after nervous system signs start.

Red Flags
  • Ascending paralysis with diaphragmatic involvement → respiratory failure — requires urgent airway/ventilatory assessment
  • Bulbar form (rare): brainstem/cranial nerve/respiratory center involvement → central respiratory paralysis
LO3 — Diagnostic Workup

CSF Findings

  • Peripheral leukocytosis, followed by CSF pleocytosis (neutrophils early, lymphocytes late)
  • Protein markedly elevated — up to 100–300× normal
  • Glucose normal
  • Initial test: PCR of stool or oropharyngeal swab for enterovirus
  • Confirmatory test: PCR of CSF, stool, or oropharyngeal samples for poliovirus RNA specifically
  • Serologic studies
  • MRI: inflammation in the ventral horn of the spinal cord
Key Differentials
ConditionDistinguishing Feature
Guillain-Barré syndromeTypically symmetric paralysis; CSF shows albuminocytologic dissociation, not pleocytosis
Other enteroviruses (e.g. EV-D68)Can also cause acute flaccid paralysis — clinically similar, differentiated by PCR typing
Acute intermittent porphyriaCan present with muscle weakness/bulbar paralysis; look for abdominal pain, psychiatric symptoms, urine color change
Spinal muscular atrophyParalysis is typically symmetric; genetic, not infectious, etiology
LO4 — Treatment
Approach

Supportive only — no antiviral treatment exists.

  • Pain relief
  • Airway management and mechanical ventilation if needed (signs of airway compromise or respiratory failure)
  • Close monitoring of blood pressure and respiratory function
LO5 — Monitoring & Complications
Acute & Long-Term Complications
  • Acute: death from diaphragmatic paralysis/respiratory failure; myocarditis
  • Long-term: residual limb weakness and contractures, chronic muscle pain, ventilatory dependency in the most severe cases (historically, "iron lung" patients)
  • Post-polio syndrome (PPS): the most frequent complication (up to 40% of survivors) — progressive muscle weakness and pain decades after the initial infection, including in muscles not originally affected

Monitoring: periodic neuromuscular follow-up in survivors (watch for emerging PPS), pulmonary function monitoring in those with a history of respiratory muscle involvement.

LO6 — Prevention & Health Promotion
Vaccination
  • Inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV): SC/IM injection; the only formulation used in routine US immunization (per ACIP schedule), alone or in combination vaccines
  • Live-attenuated oral vaccine (OPV): discontinued in the US but still used in resource-limited countries — carries the rare VDPV2 reversion risk described above
  • Additional/accelerated doses recommended for travelers to endemic regions, lab/healthcare/refugee-camp workers, and other at-risk groups
  • Basic sanitation and hygiene measures reduce fecal-oral transmission in endemic areas

Meningoencephalitis & Encephalitis of Infectious Origin

LO 1–4 Rare but Deadly Parenchymal Involvement Bacterial > Viral Mortality
How boards would word it

"A 45-year-old woman presents with 3 days of fever and headache, followed by new-onset confusion and word-finding difficulty. Her husband reports one focal seizure this morning. Temperature is 38.9°C. She is oriented to person only and has difficulty naming objects. MRI shows T2 hyperintensity in the medial temporal lobes bilaterally. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate next step?"

Answer: Start empiric IV acyclovir immediately, without waiting for HSV PCR results
What to look for: fever + altered mentation + a focal deficit (aphasia) + seizure, with bilateral medial temporal lobe involvement on MRI, is the classic pattern of HSV encephalitis. Because untreated mortality is extremely high and acyclovir is both effective and low-risk, treatment must never wait for PCR confirmation — this is the single most important teaching point for this topic.
LO1 — Natural History
Epidemiology

Several thousand cases of encephalitis are reported to the CDC each year. Untreated, encephalitis carries a mortality of 50–75%, and essentially 100% of survivors have neurologic sequelae — a genuine "rare but deadly" disease category. Worldwide: >250,000 deaths from meningitis/meningoencephalitis combined, and >89,000 deaths from encephalitis alone.

Definitions

Infection confined to the CNS parenchyma = encephalitis; infection involving both the meninges and parenchyma = meningoencephalitis. In practice, these are difficult to distinguish clinically. (Encephalitis can also be autoimmune, but this panel covers only infectious causes. Note: bacterial infection of the parenchyma is often specifically termed cerebritis.)

Etiology — Bacterial (Generally Higher Mortality/Morbidity than Viral)

Subacute

  • Mycoplasma pneumoniae
  • Listeria monocytogenes
  • Legionella pneumophila
  • Mycobacterium tuberculosis (subacute meningitis)

Chronic

  • Tuberculosis
  • Neurosyphilis (syphilis)
  • Neuroborreliosis (Lyme disease)
Etiology — Viral

Arboviruses (West Nile, Eastern/Western equine, St. Louis, Venezuelan, California), HSV-1/2, VZV, poliovirus, and HIV can all cause encephalitis — see the Viral Meningitis and Poliomyelitis panels for full detail on each. Two additional viral/protozoal etiologies specific to this topic:

Rabies Virus

RNA virus carried in the saliva of reservoir animals — even an asymptomatic animal's bite can transmit it. Ascends up peripheral nerves from the bite site to the CNS; unlike HSV, rabies has no dormant phase once it reaches the CNS, but transit time can be long (e.g., a foot bite may take up to 2 years to reach the CNS).

Clinical: malaise, headache, fever, and paresthesias around the wound → CNS excitability (violent spasms from the slightest touch, progressing to seizures) → uncontrollable pharyngeal spasms with profuse salivation ("foaming"), inability to swallow fluids ("hydrophobia") → coma and brainstem respiratory failure.

Pathology: severe diffuse edema with lymphocytic encephalitis; classic Negri body inclusions in hippocampal pyramidal cells and cerebellar Purkinje cells.

JC Virus — Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML)

Occurs in 1–6% of immunosuppressed patients; a PAPOVA virus infecting oligodendrocytes in white matter (~65% of adults show serologic exposure by age 14 — disease likely represents reactivation). Causes focal white-matter deficits (internal capsule, cerebral peduncle, medial lemniscus, cerebellar white matter).

Imaging: multifocal, non-enhancing white matter hypodensities. Pathology: demyelination with relative axon sparing, macrophages, perivascular lymphocytic cuffs, and characteristically enlarged oligodendrocytes with glassy nuclear inclusions.

Toxoplasmosis (Protozoal)

Toxoplasma gondii — ubiquitous, commonly carried asymptomatically by cats. Causes serious disease in the immunosuppressed and the fetus. Adult infection is subacute (develops over 1–2 weeks) with localizing or diffuse neurologic signs.

Imaging: multiple ring-enhancing lesions, typically at the gray-white junction and deep gray nuclei (thalamus, basal ganglia) — differential includes fungal/bacterial abscess, tuberculoma, and primary/metastatic tumor. Pathology: tiny comma-shaped organisms, free-swimming (tachyzoites) or clustered in cysts (bradyzoites).

LO2 — Clinical Presentation
Meningeal Involvement

Signs of meningeal irritation overlap with meningitis (see the Bacterial/Viral Meningitis panels) — classically elicited with Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs.

Kernig's sign — with the hip flexed, passive extension of the knee (A) or attempted straightening from 90°/90° flexion (B) produces pain/resistance
Brudzinski's sign — passive flexion of the neck (A) produces involuntary flexion of the hips and knees (B)
Signs Specific to Encephalitis (Parenchymal Involvement)
  • Acute febrile illness
  • Confusion, altered level of consciousness
  • Behavioral abnormalities, psychosis
  • Focal neurologic signs (paresis, extrapyramidal symptoms, aphasia)
  • Focal or generalized seizures
  • Hyponatremia (from hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction/SIADH)
LO3 — Diagnostic Workup
Workup
  • Lumbar puncture and CSF examination
  • PCR
  • Culture
  • CBC with differential
  • Liver function tests, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, BUN
MRI Findings
Axial MRI — active areas of inflammation (brainstem/cerebellar region)
Follow-up MRI — resolution of inflammation with appropriate treatment
LO4 — Treatment

Bacterial — Empiric Therapy

Started empirically while awaiting culture/PCR, following the same "don't delay" principle as bacterial meningitis, then narrowed once an organism is identified — e.g. macrolide/doxycycline for Mycoplasma, ampicillin for Listeria, a respiratory fluoroquinolone or macrolide (± rifampin) for Legionella, multidrug (RIPE) therapy for tuberculosis, penicillin for neurosyphilis, and doxycycline or ceftriaxone for neuroborreliosis.

Viral — Symptomatic Therapy

Mainly supportive, except when HSV encephalitis is a possibility — IV acyclovir should be started empirically without delay (see board vignette above).

Rabies — Post-Exposure Prophylaxis

Immunization (with killed or attenuated virus) started within 12–24 hours of the bite is the only chance of survival once exposure has occurred — once CNS symptoms begin, the disease is essentially always fatal.

Toxoplasmosis & PML

Toxoplasmosis: antibiotic therapy (classically pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine with leucovorin), often started empirically when suspected clinically/radiographically. PML: no specific antiviral is reliably curative; management centers on reversing the underlying immunosuppression (e.g., antiretroviral therapy in HIV, stopping an implicated immunomodulatory drug) — some antiviral regimens have been reported successful.

Brain Abscess

LO 1–4 Ring-Enhancing Lesion Headache + Fever + Focal Deficit Drainage + Antibiotics
How boards would word it

"A 38-year-old man with a history of chronic otitis media presents with 5 days of worsening headache and low-grade fever. He then has a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Examination reveals a right abducens nerve palsy. MRI shows a ring-enhancing lesion in the left temporal lobe with surrounding vasogenic edema. Blood cultures are pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?"

Answer: Consult neurosurgery for stereotactic aspiration/drainage for diagnostic sampling and therapeutic decompression, then initiate empiric antibiotics
What to look for: chronic otitis media is a classic contiguous source for a temporal lobe abscess. Headache + fever + a focal neurologic sign (here, seizure and abducens palsy) plus a ring-enhancing lesion is the textbook picture. The abducens palsy is a false localizing sign from raised ICP, not evidence the lesion is near the sixth nerve nucleus — a classic distractor. Because abscess sampling is both diagnostic (rules out tumor, guides antibiotics) and therapeutic, it's prioritized before or alongside starting antibiotics whenever feasible.
LO1 — Natural History
Epidemiology

Bacterial brain abscess incidence: ~0.3–1.3 per 100,000. Can occur at any age; in adults, male > female with a mean age of 30–40 years. In children, most common between ages 4–8 years.

Sources of abscess formation — direct inoculation (craniotomy/trauma), contiguous spread (mastoiditis shown), and hematogenous spread (septic embolus, infective endocarditis)
Routes of Entry & Organisms by Mechanism
MechanismPredisposing ConditionsCommon PathogensTypical Features
Contiguous spread (most common)Otitis media/mastoiditis (~30%+), sinusitis (~10%), odontogenic infection, meningitisStreptococcus spp., Staphylococcus spp., gram-negatives, anaerobes (esp. dental sources)Usually single, often polymicrobial; temporal lobe/cerebellum (otogenic), frontal lobe (sinus)
Hematogenous (~25%)Infective endocarditis, right-to-left cardiac shunt, distant infectious fociStaphylococcus, Streptococcus, gram-negatives (e.g. Klebsiella), HACEK organisms, anaerobesOften multiple; MCA distribution, gray-white junction
Direct inoculationHead trauma, neurosurgeryS. aureus, CoNS, S. pyogenes, anaerobesPolymicrobial
CryptogenicNo identifiable source——
Organism Frequency (Overall)

Streptococcus spp. (~40%), Enterobacteriaceae (~25%), anaerobes (~25%), Staphylococcus spp. (~10%).

Atypical/Opportunistic Pathogens (Immunocompromised Hosts)

  • Fungal: Aspergillus, Candida, Mucor, Cryptococcus neoformans
  • Nocardia spp.
  • Toxoplasma gondii (cerebral toxoplasmosis)
  • Mycobacterium tuberculosis (tuberculoma)
  • Parasites: Taenia solium (neurocysticercosis), Echinococcus (hydatid cyst)
Pathogenesis

Pre-existing anoxic/ischemic brain tissue may be necessary to "set up" an abscess. Progression:

Early cerebritis (0–5 days): neutrophil infiltration, cerebral edema
→
Late cerebritis (after 2–3 weeks): necrosis, liquefaction, macrophage infiltration
→
Fibrotic capsule forms around the lesion
General abscess-formation timeline (illustrated in skin, same underlying principle as cerebral early/late cerebritis) — infection → inflammatory response → early abscess with necrotic PMNs → mature abscess with a fibrous capsule; histology (B, C) shows the fibrous capsule walling off necrotic neutrophils ("pus")
Pathology

A localized lesion with a central core of pus and liquefactive necrosis, surrounded by a well-vascularized capsule — fibroblasts from the surrounding vessels generate reticular fibers that form this capsule — with associated brain edema around the lesion.

LO2 — Clinical Presentation
Classic Triad

Headache (~70%), fever (~50%), focal neurologic deficits (~60%) — specific deficits depend on lesion location. Presentation is often that of a nonspecific expanding intracranial lesion.

  • Symptoms of raised ICP: vomiting, papilledema, altered mental status
  • Focal neurologic deficits — commonly abducens (CN VI) or oculomotor (CN III) palsy as a false localizing sign from elevated ICP, in addition to any deficit localizing to the lesion itself
  • Generalized or focal seizures
Red Flag

A ruptured abscess presents with sudden worsening headache and meningism — a neurosurgical emergency.

LO3 — Diagnostic Workup
Axial contrast MRI — ring-enhancing lesion, left temporal lobe (in a patient with advanced otitis media)

Imaging

MRI with/without contrast (preferred): T1 — hypointense fluid, hyperintense ring, hypointense edema; T2 — hyperintense fluid, hypointense ring, hyperintense edema; DWI — hyperintense/diffusion-restricted necrotic center.

CT with contrast: hypodense necrotic center with peripheral ring enhancement.

Labs

  • ↑CRP, ↑ESR, leukocytosis
  • Blood cultures — obtain before starting antibiotics
  • HIV testing in all patients with a nontraumatic abscess
  • CSF: LP is relatively contraindicated (mass-effect/herniation risk) and not routinely performed; if obtained, may show pleocytosis, ↑protein, ↓glucose — cultures often negative
Confirmatory Test

Abscess sampling (stereotactic needle aspiration) is the diagnostic gold standard — identifies the causative organism and antibiotic sensitivities, and can be combined with therapeutic drainage. Timing: ideally within 24 hours of radiological diagnosis and before starting antibiotics. Gram stain and bacterial culture routinely; fungal culture if clinically suspected — order in consultation with infectious disease.

Differential Diagnosis of a Ring-Enhancing Lesion
ConditionDistinguishing Clue
Other CNS infectionsBacterial meningitis, epidural abscess, subdural empyema — overlapping source/risk factors
Glioblastoma / metastasisSlower, progressive course; often less fever/systemic illness; look for a known primary malignancy
Primary CNS lymphomaUsually periventricular; strongly associated with immunosuppression (e.g. HIV)
Cerebral toxoplasmosisImmunocompromised host, often multiple lesions, positive Toxoplasma IgG
Subacute hemorrhage/infarct, radiation necrosis, demyelinating plaqueDistinguished by history (recent stroke, prior radiation, MS) and lesion evolution over time
LO4 — Treatment

Antimicrobial Therapy (Empiric, with ID)

Immunocompetent: 3rd-generation cephalosporin (e.g. ceftriaxone) + metronidazole (add vancomycin if staphylococcal infection suspected).

Immunocompromised: ceftriaxone + metronidazole + voriconazole + trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

Unstable patients: start immediately. Stable patients: start within 24 hours of diagnosis, ideally after diagnostic sampling. Typical course: IV for 4–8 weeks, guided by ID and culture results.

Interventional (Drainage/Excision)

Recommended for most patients (diagnostic + therapeutic) — may be deferred for small (<2.5 cm) uncomplicated abscesses with an already-known pathogen.

Indications: all pyogenic abscesses ≥2.5 cm, abscesses causing brain shift/herniation risk, inadequate response to antimicrobials. Timing: as soon as feasible, ideally within 24 hours and before antibiotics.

Special case: in HIV-positive patients with a positive Toxoplasma IgG, drainage may be deferred in favor of presumptive toxoplasmosis treatment.

Supportive/Adjunctive Measures (from lecture notes)
  • High-dose antibiotics + neurosurgical drainage remain the core of treatment
  • Dexamethasone for elevated ICP
  • Prophylactic anticonvulsants / acute seizure management

Epidural Abscess

LO 1 only ICEA vs SEA S. aureus Most Common
How boards would word it

"A 52-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and a history of intravenous drug use is found to have an epidural abscess. Which organism is most likely responsible?"

Answer: Staphylococcus aureus
What to look for: diabetes and IV drug use are both classic risk factors for epidural abscess, and S. aureus is by far the most common causative organism overall — this pairing of risk-factor recognition with the default pathogen is the most commonly tested angle for this rare condition.
LO1 — Natural History
Definitions & Epidemiology

A suppurative infection between the dural layer and the inner table of the skull (intracranial, ICEA) or the corresponding spinal epidural space (spinal, SEA). Synonym: extradural abscess. Rare — less common than brain abscess or subdural empyema — and often a complication of head/spinal trauma, surgery, or spread from contiguous structures.

Risk Factors

  • Diabetes mellitus
  • IV drug use
  • Chronic alcohol abuse
  • Recent spinal trauma, surgery, or epidural anesthesia
  • HIV infection
  • Untreated otitis or sinusitis

Pathogenesis

Most commonly hematogenous spread to the epidural space via the vertebral venous plexus.

  • Staphylococcus aureus — most common organism overall
  • Tuberculosis — still a common cause of spinal infection in resource-limited settings
  • ICEA: typically polymicrobial, but can favor Streptococcus
  • SEA: more often Staphylococcus
Pathology

Located between the dura and the surrounding bone. Stages: bacterial seeding (hematogenous, direct invasion, or inoculation) → inflammation with pus and granulation tissue → neural damage by compression.

Acute

Rapidly forming (~2 weeks), thick purulent exudate — typically posterior to the cord.

Chronic

Typically spreads from vertebral osteomyelitis — located anterior to the cord, with dense granulation tissue and fibrosis.

Subdural Empyema

LO 1–2 Frontal Sinusitis → Most Cases Can Deteriorate Rapidly
How boards would word it

"A 16-year-old boy with a 10-day history of frontal sinusitis presents with fever, severe headache, and new-onset left-sided weakness. Over the next several hours he becomes progressively more lethargic, then unresponsive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Subdural empyema
What to look for: frontal sinusitis is the classic antecedent for subdural empyema, and the rapid progression from a focal deficit to obtundation/coma — rather than the more indolent course seen after trauma or surgery — is characteristic when the empyema arises from sinusitis or mastoiditis. Suspect SDE in any sinusitis patient who develops new neurologic signs.
LO1 — Natural History
Epidemiology

Rare — accounts for ~15–25% of focal suppurative CNS infections, or ~20–33% of all intracranial infections by some estimates. More common in children and young adults, with a male-to-female ratio of 3:1.

Sources

  • Frontal sinusitis — the vast majority of cases
  • Mastoiditis / otitis media
  • Surgical intervention, trauma
  • Meningitis
  • Seeding of a pre-existing subdural hematoma

Organisms

Streptococcus spp. (especially the S. milleri group), Staphylococcus aureus, anaerobic organisms, Enterobacteriaceae, and gram-negative bacteria.

Pathogenesis — Two Routes of Spread
Direct extension through valveless emissary veins of the cranium (relatively uncommon)
Indirect extension via septic thrombophlebitis of mucosal/communicating veins (the more common route)
Pathology

A collection of pus in the subdural space — the potential space between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater.

LO2 — Clinical Presentation

Early Stage

  • Fever
  • Progressively worsening headache

Later Stages

  • Focal neurologic signs — hemiplegia is the most common
  • Seizures
  • Nuchal rigidity, signs of increased ICP
Tempo Depends on Etiology

Empyemas arising from sinusitis or mastoiditis are often associated with seizures, focal deficits, and rapid deterioration of consciousness — progressing from obtundation to coma. Empyemas secondary to prior trauma or surgery tend to be more clinically indolent.

Pearl

Subdural empyema should be suspected in any patient with sinusitis who subsequently develops neurologic signs or symptoms.

Neurosyphilis

LO 1–2 Tertiary Syphilis Argyll-Robertson Pupil The Great Imitator
How boards would word it

"A 58-year-old man presents with a 1-year history of progressive personality change, memory loss, and grandiose delusions. His wife also reports a slapping, unsteady gait that is worse in the dark. On exam, his pupils constrict with accommodation but fail to react to light. Deep tendon reflexes are absent at the ankles, and proprioception is impaired bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Neurosyphilis (paretic neurosyphilis with concurrent tabes dorsalis)
What to look for: grandiose delusions plus progressive dementia (paretic neurosyphilis, historically "general paresis of the insane") combined with a sensory ataxic gait and absent reflexes (tabes dorsalis) is the classic combination. The Argyll-Robertson pupil — accommodates but does not react to light — clinches the diagnosis; this specific pattern of light-near dissociation is distinct from other pupillary syndromes (e.g. Marcus Gunn, Adie's, Horner's).
▶
▶ Neurosyphilis
Video — "Neurosyphilis" (YouTube)
LO1 — Natural History
Epidemiology

Neurosyphilis can occur at any stage of infection (~0.8% of early syphilis cases) and is more common in states of immunosuppression — HIV coinfection both predisposes to acquiring syphilis and can accelerate its course. Historically: incidence fell sharply after penicillin's introduction (1940s), rose again in the mid-1980s (IV drug use/crack cocaine, sex-for-drugs, anonymous sex, multiple partners) — rates doubled from 1986–1990, peaking at 53.8 cases/100,000 in 1990 — then declined to an all-time low by 2000 (increased awareness, aggressive screening, primary prevention). Case counts have been rising again since (e.g. a rate increase of 2.5→2.7 per 100,000 from 2003–2004).

Life Cycle of Treponema pallidum
Spirochete penetrates skin/mucosa (contact with an infectious chancre)
→
Primary chancre forms, heals spontaneously in weeks (often no care sought)
→
Secondary stage (months–years later): transient lymphocytic meningitis + rash (palms/soles), self-limited
→
Long asymptomatic latency (5–20 years)
→
Tertiary syphilis: aortitis + neurosyphilis (in ~10% of patients)
Pathogenesis

T. pallidum invades the CNS and crosses the blood-brain barrier → sets up immune-driven inflammation in the meninges → invades the walls of CNS blood vessels, causing endothelial swelling, ischemia, and obliteration of small vessels → final stage: invasion of neurons in the cerebrum (→ dementia) and the dorsal root ganglia (→ tabes dorsalis).

Pathology
  • Lymphocytic pleocytosis in the CSF
  • Diffuse meningeal inflammation (months–years post-infection) — evident in only ~25% of cases
  • Obliterative endarteritis (years post-infection)
  • General paresis (late-forming): widespread cortical neuronal death with numerous microglia — the classic "windswept cortex" histologic appearance — and subsequent cortical atrophy
  • Tabes dorsalis (20+ years post-infection): complete loss of proprioception and discriminative touch from loss of large-caliber dorsal root ganglion neurons, with demyelination and gliosis of the dorsal columns — the resulting scarring contracts the tissue, flattening the dorsal surface of the cord
  • Gumma: a syphilitic granuloma that can affect the CNS (or any organ) and act as a mass lesion
LO2 — Clinical Presentation
Overall Pattern

An insidious but progressive loss of mental and physical function, accompanied by mood alterations — highly variable presentation has earned syphilis the nickname "the great imitator." Clinical features can range from acute syphilitic meningitis (neck stiffness, nausea) to subacute stroke/meningitis/cranial nerve disorders, through to the three classic chronic entities below.

Meningovascular Syphilis

Obliterative endarteritis + perivascular inflammation → can present as subacute stroke, meningitis, or cranial nerve disorders.

Paretic Neurosyphilis ("General Paresis")

Chronic, progressive meningoencephalitis from widespread parenchymal invasion → cerebral atrophy and major neurocognitive disorder. Early: personality change, memory/judgment deficits, mood alterations (including delusions of grandeur), progressing to severe dementia. Can include dysarthria, hypotonia, tremors. "General paresis of the insane" historically describes the combined dementia + paralysis picture.

Tabes Dorsalis

Damage to the dorsal roots/dorsal columns → impaired proprioception and vibration sense → sensory (broad-based) ataxia, positive Romberg sign, absent deep tendon reflexes, "lightning pains" and dysesthesias (mainly lower extremities), and Charcot joints from repeated unrecognized joint injury.

Argyll-Robertson pupil — bilateral miosis with irregular pupils; pupillary light reflex absent, but accommodation reflex present ("ARP")
Pearl

Neurosyphilis was historically the most common cause of dementia and, with rising incidence in immunosuppressed populations, remains an important entry on the dementia differential today.

Prion Disease

LO 1–2 No Nucleic Acid Self-Propagating Misfolding Rapid Course
How boards would word it

"A 62-year-old woman is brought in by her family for a 3-month history of rapidly worsening memory loss and personality change. Over the past few weeks she has developed sudden, brief jerking movements of her limbs and an unsteady gait. She is now largely unresponsive and immobile despite appearing awake. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
What to look for: rapidly progressive dementia unfolding over weeks-to-months (not the years typical of Alzheimer's), plus myoclonus and ataxia progressing to akinetic mutism, is the classic sCJD picture. The pace of decline — death typically within ~7 months of onset — is what most sharply separates this from other causes of dementia on boards.
▶
▶ Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD): An Overview of Symptoms, Causes, & Diagnosis
Video — "Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD): An Overview of Symptoms, Causes, & Diagnosis" (YouTube)
LO1 — Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

Prion diseases are caused by infectious proteins that cause neuronal death and degeneration — in essence, degenerative diseases with an infectious origin. The most common form is Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD): relentlessly and rapidly progressive, resulting in dementia. Synonym: transmissible spongiform encephalopathy — "-opathy" rather than "-itis" is the more precise/standard term, since this is a non-inflammatory degenerative process rather than a true infectious inflammation.

Incidence ~1 in 1,000,000. Exact transmission mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Sporadic CJD (sCJD) — the most common form — presents in the 50–70 year age range.

Etiology

Disease results from the spread of a misfolded protein that behaves as though it were infectious — self-propagating without any genetic material. Three recognized forms:

  • Sporadic — no identifiable source (most common, e.g. sCJD)
  • Inherited — germline PrP gene mutations
  • Transmitted (acquired) — iatrogenic or dietary exposure
Pathogenesis
PrPC — normal membrane-bound protein, α-helix conformation, function unknown
→
Conformational change to PrPSc ("scrapie") — abnormal β-pleated sheet
→
PrPSc binds native PrPC and converts it into more PrPSc (self-propagating)
→
Accumulates in neuronal membranes, lysosomes, and cytoplasm
→
Neuronal cell death
  • Prions contain no nucleic acid — a defining and unique feature among infectious agents
  • PrPSc is resistant to digestion by cellular enzymes (protease-resistant), which contributes to its accumulation and persistence
Pathology
  • Spongiform degeneration — vacuolation giving the tissue a characteristic "spongy" appearance; the pathologic hallmark of prion disease
  • Amyloid plaque formation
Classification (Variant Forms from PrP Mutations)

Sporadic CJD

No identifiable source; most common form.

Variant CJD

Linked to dietary exposure (e.g. bovine spongiform encephalopathy/"mad cow disease").

Iatrogenic CJD

Transmitted via medical procedures (e.g. contaminated instruments/tissue grafts).

Fatal Familial Insomnia

Inherited; progressive, ultimately fatal insomnia with autonomic dysfunction.

Sporadic Fatal Insomnia

Non-inherited counterpart of fatal familial insomnia.

Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker Syndrome

Inherited; slower course, prominent cerebellar ataxia.

Kuru

Historically transmitted via ritual cannibalism (Papua New Guinea); now essentially extinct.

LO2 — Clinical Presentation
Sporadic CJD
  • Onset age 50–70
  • Rapid progression — death within ~7 months of onset
  • Rapidly progressive memory and behavioral changes leading to dementia
  • Myoclonus and ataxia can develop
  • Terminates in akinetic mutism
Pearl

The single most useful feature for distinguishing sCJD from other dementias is its pace — progression over weeks to a few months, versus the years-long courses typical of Alzheimer's or other neurodegenerative dementias.
